title: Definition
body_md: Let $f_{1}\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right),\ldots,f_{m}\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right):\mathbb{N}^{n}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$. We say that the configuration $\{f_{1}\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right),\ldots,f_{m}\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right)\}$ is partition regular on $\mathbb{N}$ (PR from now on) if for all finite partitions $\mathbb{N}=A_{1}\cup\ldots\cup A_{k}$ there are $i\leq k$ and $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $j\leq m$ $f_{j}\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right)\in A_{i}$.

label: def:fp
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:fp} Let $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$. We say that $f$ is a factor-picking function if
\begin{enumerate}
\item for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ $f(n)$ divides $n$;
\item for all $n,m\in\mathbb{N}$ $f(n^{m})=f(n)$.
\end{enumerate}
Given a factor-picking $f$, we say that $e_{f}:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ is its exact exponent if for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ 
\[e_{f}(n)=\begin{cases} 1, & \text{if} \ f(n)=1;\\
\max\{m\in\mathbb{N}\mid f(n)^{m}\ \text{divides} \ n\}, &\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]

We say that ${p}\in\beta\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N}$ is $f$-highly exponential if for all $g:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ 
\[\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid g(f(n))<e_{f}(n)\}\in p.\]

Finally, we say that $p$ is highly exponential if it is $f$-highly exponential for all factor picking functions with $f(p)\neq 1$.

title: Definition
body_md: Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\beta(\mathbb{N}^{n})$. We say that $\alpha\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}^{n}$ is a generator of $p$ if, for all $A\in p$, $\alpha\in\,^{\ast}A$. In this case we will write that $p=p_{\alpha}$ or, equivalently, that $\alpha\models p$. We let $\mu(p)$ denote the set of generators of $p$, and write $\alpha\sim\beta$ whenever $\alpha,\beta$ generate the same ultrafilter.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $p\in\beta(\mathbb{N}^{2})$, $q,r\in\beta\mathbb{N}$. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] The product $q\times r$ is the filter generated by sets $A\times B$ for $A\in q$, $B\in r$.
\item[(b)] An ultrafilter $p$ is the tensor product of $q,r$ (notation: $p=q\otimes r$) if for all $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2}$ we have that
\[A\in p\Leftrightarrow \{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid \{m\in\mathbb{N}\mid (n,m)\in A\}\in r\}\in q.\]
\end{enumerate}
A pair $(\alpha,\beta)\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}$ will be called a tensor pair if it generates a tensor product.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Let $\alpha,\beta\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}$. We say that $\alpha\ll\beta$ if for all $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ we have that $f(\alpha)<\beta$. We let ${\rm er}(\alpha):=\{f(\alpha)\mid f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}\}\setminus\mathbb{N}$.

label: lem:list
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:list} Let $p,q\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ $r\in\beta(\mathbb{N}^{2})$, let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}$, let $f,g:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$. The following facts hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item\label{T1} If $\alpha\sim \beta$ and $h:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}^k$, then $h(\alpha)\sim h(\beta)$.
\item\label{T2} If $f(\alpha)\sim\beta$, then there exists $\alpha^{\prime}\sim\alpha$ with $f(\alpha^{\prime})=\beta$.
\item\label{T3} If $f(\alpha)\sim \alpha$, then $f(\alpha)=\alpha$.
\item\label{T4} The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f(\alpha)\sim g(\beta)$.
\item There exists $\beta'\sim \beta$ such that $f(\alpha)= g(\beta')$.
\end{enumerate}
\item\label{T5} $(\alpha,\beta)$ is a tensor pair if and only if for all $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ we have $f(\beta)\in\mathbb{N}$ or $\alpha<f(\beta)$.
\item\label{T6} For all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $(n,\alpha)$ and $(\alpha,n)$ are tensor pairs.
\item\label{T7} If $(\alpha,\beta)$ is a tensor pair, then $p_{(\alpha,\beta)}=p_{\alpha}\otimes p_{\beta}$.
\item\label{T8} If $r\supseteq p_{\alpha}\times p_{\beta}$, then for all $(\eta,\sigma)\in \mu(r)$ we have $\eta\sim\alpha,\sigma\sim\beta$.
\item\label{T9} If $r\supseteq p_{\alpha}\times p_{\beta}$, there exist $\alpha^{\prime}\sim\alpha$, $\beta^{\prime}\sim \beta$ such that $(\alpha,\beta^{\prime})\sim (\alpha^{\prime},\beta)\in\mu(r)$.
\item\label{T10} If $(\alpha,\beta)$ is a tensor pair, then so is $(f(\alpha),g(\beta))$.
\item\label{T11} If $(\alpha,\beta)$ is a tensor pair, with $\beta\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N}$, then $\alpha\ll\beta$. The converse does not hold.
\item\label{T12} $\alpha\ll \beta\gamma$ if and only if $\alpha\ll \beta$ or $\alpha\ll\gamma$.
\item\label{T13} Let $\gamma\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}$. If $\alpha\leq\beta\ll\gamma\leq\delta$ then $\alpha\ll\delta$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{T1}-\ref{T2}-\ref{T3} These are well known trivial facts, see e.g. \cite[Proposition 11.2.4-Theorem 11.2.7]{DN}.
		
		\ref{T4} This is a particular istance of \ref{T2}.

    \ref{T5} This is Puritz's Theorem, see \cite{P2}.

    \ref{T6} This is immediate from \ref{T5}.
    
    \ref{T7}-\ref{T8} These are immediate, see \cite[Proposition 4.6]{luperi2019nonstandard}.

    \ref{T9} This is a standard saturation argument, see e.g. \cite[Proposition 2.3.(viii)]{gasparroluperi26}.

    \ref{T10} This is a rephrasing of \cite[Theorem 4.15.(7)]{luperi2019nonstandard}

    \ref{T11} If $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ is such that $f(\alpha)>\beta$, the function $g:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ defined by $g(n)=\min \{m\in\mathbb{N}\mid f(m)>n\}$ is such that $g(\beta)\leq\alpha$, $g(\beta)\notin\mathbb{N}$, contradicting \ref{T5}. The converse does not hold because, e.g, if $(\alpha,\beta)$ and $(\beta,\gamma)$ are tensor, then $2^{\alpha}3^{\beta}\ll 2^{\beta}3^{\gamma}$ but the $2$-adic valuation of the latter is smaller than the former, contradicting \ref{T5}.

\ref{T12} Right to left is immediate. As for left to right, assume the opposite, that there are $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ and $g:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ such that $ f(\alpha)\geq \beta$ and $ g(\alpha)\geq \gamma$. If we define $h(n)=f(n)\cdot g(n)$, clearly $ h(\alpha)\geq \beta\gamma$, a contradiction.

\ref{T13}. Assume that $f(\alpha)\geq\delta$. Let $h:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ be the function mapping $n$ to $\max\{f(m)\mid m\leq n\}$. Then $h(\beta)\geq f(\alpha)\geq \gamma$, against $\beta\ll\gamma$.

title: Definition
body_md:
For $n\in{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{1\}$, we let the principal exponent of $n$ (denoted by $PE(n)$) to be the largest $b\in{\mathbb{N}}$ such that there exists $a\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n=a^b$. Moreover, we let the principal basis of $n$ (denoted by $PB(n)$) to be the unique $a\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n=a^{PE(n)}$. For $n=1$ we let $PB(1)=PE(1)=1$.

We also let the radical of $n$ (notation: ${\rm rad}(n)$) to be the product of the prime divisors of $n$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{E1}$\Rightarrow$\ref{E2}$\Rightarrow$\ref{E5} and \ref{E3}$\Rightarrow$\ref{E4} are obvious.

\ref{E2}$\Rightarrow$\ref{E3} Let $\alpha\in\mu(p)$ be such that ${\rm rad}(\alpha)\ll e_{{\rm rad}}(\alpha)$. For all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ ${\rm rad}(n)\leq PB(n)$ and $e_{{\rm rad}}(n)\geq PE(n)$. By transfer, ${\rm rad}(\alpha)\leq PB(\alpha)$ and $e_{\rm rad}(\alpha)\geq PE(\alpha)$, and we conclude by Lemma \ref{lem:list}.\ref{T13}.

\ref{E5}$\Rightarrow$\ref{E2} Let $f$ be factor-picking such that ${\rm rad}(\alpha)\mid f(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha\models p$, so $\{n\in\mathbb{N}\in{\rm rad}(n)\mid f(n)\}\in p$. Hence $\{n\in\mathbb{N}:e_{\rm rad}(n)\geq e_f(n)\}\in p$ and consequently $e_{\rm rad}(\alpha)\geq e_f(\alpha)$. Thus $f(\alpha)\ll e_{f}(\alpha)$ implies ${\rm rad}(\alpha)\ll e_{\rm rad}(\alpha)$.

\ref{E4}$\Rightarrow$\ref{E1} Let $f$ be a factor-picking function. $f(\alpha^{\beta})=f(\alpha)\ll\beta$ by hypothesis, whilst $e_{f}(\alpha^{\beta})=\beta\cdot e_{f}(\alpha)\geq \beta$. We conclude again by Lemma \ref{lem:list}.\ref{T13}.

label: highexp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{highexp}
Let $\alpha=\prod_{i\leq z}p_i^{k_i}$. Let $f$ be a factor-picking function and $e_{f}$ its exact exponent. If $f(\alpha)\ll e_{f}(\alpha)$ then, for all $i\leq z$ such that $p_{i}$ divides $f(\alpha)$, $p_i\ll k_i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For all $i\leq z$ such that $p_{i}$ divides $f(\alpha)$ we have $p_{i}\leq f(\alpha)$ and similarly $k_{i}\geq e_{f}(\alpha)$; thus, $p_{i}\leq f(\alpha)\ll e_{f}(\alpha)\leq k_{i}$, from which $p_{i}\ll k_{i}$ follows immediately.
head: environment

label: exweakhe
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exweakhe}
The reverse implication does not hold, in the following sense. Take $p_1,p_2$ infinite nonstandard primes, and $k_1,k_2\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}$ such that $p_1\ll k_1<p_2\ll k_2$. If $\alpha=p_1^{k_{1}}p_{2}^{k_{2}}$, then ${\rm rad}(\alpha)=p_1p_2$ and $e_{\rm rad}(\alpha)=k_1$, so ${\rm rad}(\alpha)>e_{\rm rad}(\alpha)$.

label: FundRemCut
title: Lemma

title: Definition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Let ${p}$ be highly exponential and generated by $\gamma_{2}$, and let $q$ be generated by $\gamma_{1}=\prod_{i\leq z}p_i^{k_i}$, with ${\rm rad}(\gamma_{1})=\eta_{1} | \eta_{2} ={\rm rad}(\gamma_{2})$. Since an internal set bounded from above has a maximum, let $\mu_1=\max\{k_i:i\leq z\}$, so $\gamma_{1} | \eta_{1}^{\mu_{1}}$. By Lemma \ref{FundRemCut}, pick $\mu_{2}>\mu_{1}$ with $\eta_{2}^{\mu_{2}}\sim\gamma_{2}$. With this choice we have that $\eta_{1}^{\mu_{1}}|\eta_{2}^{\mu_{2}}$, hence $\gamma_{1}| \eta_{2}^{\mu_{2}}$, as desired.

(ii) By contrast, assume that $p$ is not highly exponential. Let $\alpha\models PB(p),\alpha^{\beta}\models p$ and let $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be such that $\beta<f(\alpha)$. Let $h$ be the function mapping $n$ to the maximal exponent appearing in the prime factorization of $n$, and let $g=h\cdot f$. In particular, $\beta<g(\alpha)$. Let $q$ be such that ${\rm rad}(\alpha)^{g(\alpha)}\models q$. Then ${\rm rad}(p)={\rm rad}(q)$, hence by hypothesis some generator $\delta$ of $q$ divides $\alpha^{\beta}$. But generators of $q$ have the form ${\rm rad}(\gamma)^{g(\gamma)}$ for some $\gamma\sim \alpha$, and ${\rm rad}(\gamma)^{g(\gamma)}|\alpha^{\beta}$ entails that ${\rm rad}(\gamma)|\alpha^{\beta}$. As all primes in the factorization of ${\rm rad}(\gamma)$ have exponent $1$, this entails that ${\rm rad}(\gamma)|{\rm rad}(\alpha)$; since ${\rm rad}(p)$ does not strictly divide itself, this forces $\gamma=\alpha$. Hence ${\rm rad}(\alpha)^{g(\alpha)}|\alpha^{\beta}$, which is impossible as it would give $g(\alpha)=h(\alpha)\cdot f(\alpha)\leq h(\alpha)\cdot \beta$, hence $f(\alpha)\leq\beta$.

title: Corollary
body_md: Let $p\in\beta\mathbb{N}$. If $rad(p)$ does not strictly divide itself then $p$ is highly exponential if and only if, for all $q\in \beta\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$, if $rad(q)=rad(p)$ then $q$ divides $p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This is immediate from Theorem \ref{alphthm:A}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: If ${\rm rad}(p)$ strictly divides itself, the implication $(ii)\Rightarrow (i)$ is, in general, false. Let $p_{i}$ be the increasing enumeration of the primes, and let $p$ be generated by $\eta=p_{1}^{\alpha} \cdot p_{2}^{\alpha-1}\cdot\ldots\cdot p_{\alpha}$ for some infinite $\alpha$; clearly, ${\rm rad}(p)$ strictly divides itself. Notice that $\eta=f(\alpha)$ for $f$ a standard function; moreover, $p$ is not highly exponential (in fact, quite the opposite is true, as $PB(p)=p$). However, $p$ is maximal with respect to the divisibility. In fact, pick any $q\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ and let $\beta$ be a generator of $q$. Pick $\gamma\sim \alpha$ with $(\beta,\gamma)$ tensor. Then it is immediate to see that $\beta|p_{1}^{\gamma}\cdot\ldots\cdot p_{\gamma}=f(\gamma)\sim f(\alpha)$.

title: Remark
body_md: It follows directly from the definition that $E_1({p},{q})$ and $E_2({p},{q})$ respectively are images of the tensor product ${p}\otimes{q}$ via extensions to $\beta(\mathbb{N}^2)$ of functions $(n,m)\mapsto n^m$ and $(n,m)\mapsto m^n$. Hence, for $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mu(p\otimes q)$ we have that $\alpha^{\beta}\in \mu(E_{1}(p,q))$, whilst $\beta^{\alpha}\in\mu (E_{2}(p,q))$.

head: manual

title: Example
body_md:
Let $p,q$ be nonprincipal ultrafilters, with $p$ containing the complement of the set of perfect powers. Let $(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1})\in \mu(p\otimes q), (\beta_{2},\alpha_{2})\in\mu(q\otimes p)$. As $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}$ are not perfect powers, we have that $\alpha_{1}=PB(\alpha_{1}^{\beta_{1}})$, $\alpha_{2}=PB(\alpha_{2}^{\beta_{2}})$. If 
\[X=\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid PB(n)<PE(n)\},\]
we have that $\alpha_{1}^{\beta_{1}}\in\,^{\ast}X$, whilst $\alpha_{2}^{\beta_{2}}\in\,^{\ast}X^{c}$. Hence $E_{1}(p,q)\neq E_{2}(q,p)$.
head: environment

label: eq: paireq
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\alpha$ be a generator of $p$. Let $\beta_{1}<\beta_{2}$ be generators of $q$ with $(\beta_{1},\alpha),(\alpha,\beta_{2})$ tensor pairs, so that $\alpha^{\beta_{2}}$ generates $E_1({p},{q})$ and $\alpha^{\beta_{1}}$ generates $E_{2}(q,p)$. Notice that $f(\alpha^{\beta_{1}})=f(\alpha)=f(\alpha^{\beta_{2}})$, whilst $e_f(\alpha^{\beta_1})=e_f(\alpha)\beta_1$, $e_{f}(\alpha^{\beta_{2}})=e_{f}(\alpha)\beta_{2}$. As $E_1({p},{q})=E_2({q},{p})$, we have that $\alpha^{\beta_{1}}\sim\alpha^{\beta_{2}}$. Applying the function $(f,e_{f})$ to $\alpha^{\beta_{1}}$ and $\alpha^{\beta_{2}}$, we deduce by Lemma \ref{lem:list}.\ref{T1} that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq: paireq}\tag{$\diamond$} (f(\alpha),e_{f}(\alpha)\beta_{1})\sim (f(\alpha),e_{f}(\alpha)\beta_{2}).\end{equation}
(i) By Lemma \ref{lem:list}.\ref{T10}, $(f(\alpha),\beta_{2})$ is a tensor pair, hence $f(\alpha)\ll \beta_{2}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:list}.\ref{T12}, it follows that $f(\alpha)\ll e_{f}(\alpha)\beta_{2}$. By (\ref{eq: paireq}), it follows that $f(\alpha)\ll e_{f}(\alpha)\beta_{1}$. But $(\beta_{1},f(\alpha))$ is a tensor pair by Lemma \ref{lem:list}.\ref{T10}, hence $f(\alpha)\not\ll \beta_{1}$. Again from Lemma \ref{lem:list}.\ref{T12} we deduce hence that $f(\alpha)\ll e_{f}(\alpha)$. 

(ii) By (\ref{eq: paireq}), $e_{f}(\alpha)\beta_{1}\sim e_{f}(\alpha)\beta_{2}$. We conclude as, by Lemma \ref{lem:list}.\ref{T10}, $(e_{f}(\alpha),\beta_{2}),(\beta_{1},e_{f}(\alpha))$ are tensor pairs, hence $e_{f}(\alpha)\beta_{2}$ generates $e_{f}(p)\odot{q}$ whilst $\beta_{1}e_{f}(\alpha)$ generates ${q}\odot e_{f}({p})$.

label: ReformulationRm
title: Remark
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $\eta\notin er(\mu)$, with $\mu>\eta$. Let $\alpha=\mu^{\eta},\beta=\frac{\mu!}{\eta}$. Then $\alpha\notin er(\alpha^{\beta})$: in fact, $\alpha^{\beta}=\mu^{\mu!}$. As $\mu^{\mu!}$ is clearly a function of $\mu$, $\alpha\in er(\mu^{\mu!})$ would entail $\alpha\in er(\mu)$, namely $\mu^{\eta}\in er(\mu)$, from which clearly $\eta\in er(\mu)$. Notice that $\alpha^{\beta}$ can be written as an exponential in uncountably many ways.

Let us notice, however, that $\alpha\in er(\alpha^{\beta})$ is possible. This happens, e.g., when $\alpha$ is not a perfect power, in which case $\alpha=PB(\alpha^{\beta})$ for all $\beta$. It also happens whenever $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ is such that there is some $k\in\mathbb{N}$ for which $|\{m\in\mathbb{N}:m^{f(m)}=n\}|\leq k$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. In such a case, by transfer we have that for all $\alpha\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}$ $|\{\beta\in\,^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}}:\beta^{f(\beta)}=\alpha\}|\leq k$, hence if we let $g_i:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ be the function mapping every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ to the $i$-th smallest number $m$ such that $m^{f(m)}=n$, then every $\alpha\in\,^{\ast}{\mathbb{N}}$ is equal to $\,^{\ast} g_i(\alpha^{\,^{\ast} f(\alpha)})$ for some $i$, and so $\alpha\in{\rm er}(\alpha^{\,^{\ast} f(\alpha)})$. This case includes all polynomial functions $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$.

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $\alpha,\beta\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N}$. Then $\alpha\in er\left(\alpha^{\beta}\right)$ if and only if $\beta\in er\left(\alpha^{\beta}\right)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $\alpha=f(\alpha^{\beta})$, then the set $A=\{n\in\mathbb{N}:(\exists m\in\mathbb{N})f(n)^m=n\}$ belongs to the ultrafilter generated by $\alpha^{\beta}$. Let $g:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be the function mapping $n$ to $1$ if $n\notin A$, and to the unique $m$ such that $n=f(n)^{m}$ if $n\in A$. Then, trivially, $\beta=g(\alpha^\beta)$. The converse is similar.

label: pfree
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{pfree} Let $p$ be generated by $\alpha^{f(\alpha)}$ for some non perfect power $\alpha$. For $i=1,2$ let $\pi_{i}:\mathbb{N}^{2}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be the projection on the $i$-th coordinate. Then, for all distinct $q_{1},q_{2}\in\beta\mathbb{N}^2$ such that $\pi_1(q_1)=\pi_1(q_2)=p$ we have $E(q_{1})\neq E(q_{2})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Assume the opposite, that $E(q_{1})=E(q_{2})$. Let $(\alpha_{i},\beta_{i})\in\mu (q_{i})$ for $i=1,2$ be such that $\alpha_1^{\beta_1}=\alpha_2^{\beta_2}$. As $p$ is generated by $\alpha^{f(\alpha)}$ for some $\alpha\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}$, it follows that there are non perfect powers $\alpha_{3}\sim\alpha_{4}\in\,^{\ast}\mathbb{N}$ so that $\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{i+2}^{f(\alpha_{i+2})}$ for $i=1,2$. Hence $\alpha_3^{f(\alpha_{3})\beta_1}=\alpha_4^{f(\alpha_{4})\beta_2}$ which, as $\alpha_{3}$ and $\alpha_{4}$ are not perfect powers, forces $\alpha_{3}=\alpha_{4}$, hence $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}$. Therefore $q_{1}=q_{2}$.
